title: Setting up Git
text:
Before you start, check whether you already have git:

# Request the path to your git.exe
which git

# Request the version of your git installation
git --version

if the return is something like the message below you need to install it.

git: command not found


Mac users may be prompted help immediately and they should accept.
If you are not offered to have it installed for you, install it manually:

visit https://git-scm.com/install/
find the right version for your local machine (Mac, Linux)

On Linux

sudo apt-add-repository ppa:git-core/ppa
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install git


# keep it up to date
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install git

On Mac via Homebrew

brew install git

# keep it up to date
brew update && brew upgrade git

On Windows, install gitforwindows. It comes with the Git bash which gives access to the Bash shell in addition to git. If you already have git installed, it may be good to update it (via shell/git command line)

git update-git-for-windows

title: Setting up Git
text:
2 Configure your credentials
Below you will need an account with GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket (or similar). When asked to enter your user.email, use the one you have registered with a host server. Your user.name can be anything you feel comfortable with, but best is your actual name. If you don’t want to sign up to a host server, you can use anything that looks like a valid email address. It will be stored in the metadata of the commits.

2.1 via command line
Now you have to decide on an email-address and a name you want git to associate with you. We can do this via the command line (bash shell):

$ git config --global user.name "John Doe"
$ git config --global user.email johndoe@example.com



2.2 in R via usethis
We can also do it in R via the usethis (or devtools) package

library(usethis) ## or library(devtools)
use_git_config(
  user.name = "Jane Doe", 
  user.email = "jane@example.com"
  )

# check by running a git situation-report:
# - your user.name and user.email should appear in global Git config
git_sitrep()


# to connect to GitHub you need a PAT (personal access token):
usethis::create_github_token()

# Now put your PAT into the git credentials store:
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()



2.3 in Visual Studio Code
In VSC git can be used via the Source Control panel. To connect your repository to github, you need to:

open the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) and run Publish to GitHub
Sign in when prompted and return to VSC
Enter an available repository name and chose private or public
Make changes in your folder
stage (add) and commit them to the repository
push them to GitHub

title: Version control & Git
text:
Git: three main concepts

Snapshot: save a meaningful state of your project.
Compare: see exactly what changed, and when.
Recover: return to a known-good state when an experiment goes sideways.

Git is not a backup folder. It is a timeline of deliberate project snapshots.

title: Version control & Git
text:
Vocabulary1

Version Control A system for maintaining current and past copies of all of your files and a record of all the changes you have made;
git Version control software for tracking your project on your local computer
GitHub A free, public remote website where your project is permanently hosted
Repository Any collection of files that belong to the same project, plus a few special git files that set up the version control. Also called a repo by hipster programmers.
Clone Create a local copy of a repository from the GitHub website to your own website. You can clone from your own repository or anyone else’s that is posted on GitHub. Once the files are on your local computer you can edit or use them as you like. However, you can only change files on GitHub for the repositories that you yourself created or for projects that you have been invited to collaborate on with others.
Commit (the noun) A snapshot of your file system at a particular time. Since your last commit, it keeps track of the files you currently have, the ones you have deleted or added, and any changes you have made to files. Each commit has a unique identifier (“SHA”)
Commit (the verb) When you commit, you are taking a snapshot of your files at the current time. You must add a summary of the commit that briefly describes what changes you have made (such as “add new homework file”). Note that all commits affect only the local copy of your repository. They do not affect the remote copy that is stored on GitHub
Push Pushing a set of changes means copying them from your local repository up to GitHub.
Pull(=fetch) Pulling means copying the repository in its current state on GitHub down to your local repository. This would incorporate any changes that others have made (and pushed) in a collaborative project.

Gotelli (2025)

title: Version control & Git
text:
Git is language-agnostic
Git does not care whether the file is Python, R, Bash, Markdown, or a dataset.
project/
├── analysis.py
├── model.R
├── run.sh
├── report.qmd
└── data/
    └── observations.csv
Git tracks files and their history. Your Python environment, R packages, and shell are separate concerns that we can record alongside the code (e.g., in R using renv lockfiles or in python using requirements.txt files)

title: Version control & Git

text:
Three places where a change can live








Place
Meaning
Git command




Working folder
Your files right now. You can edit, run, and inspect them.
git status , git diff


Staging area
A review basket: the exact changes you want in the next snapshot.
git add


Repository
The saved timeline of snapshots, called commits.
git commit

title: Version control & Git
text:
Git or GitHub?



Git


local software (offline)
tracks file changes
needs to be installed (it’s free)
works natively in the terminal


GitHub


Remote code hosting and collaboration platform (owned by Microsoft)
Common alternatives: Bitbucket and GitLab (some instances are self-hosted by universities)
Additional features include collaboration, project management, publishing, and Actions
Free account required
Works via the web, terminal, and GUI clients (such as GitHub Desktop)

text:
Benefits1 of web-hosting on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or similar


Organizing, recording, and disseminating your work - exposure prevents neglecting these tasks
Structured collaboration and access to powerful tools for asynchronous work
Creating web sites in 60 seconds
Can be turned into citable content (add CITATION.txt file or connect to Zenodo and get a DOI)
Acts as shareable lab notebook for computational work


Bryan (2018)

title: Version control & Git
text:
Workflows in Git(Hub)
After initializing a folder as a git repository (git init or git clone)

Create files, make changes
git status
stage changes: git add -A
commit to make a snapshot: git commit -am "Commit Message"
Do this frequently!
git status
Upload commits to GitHub: git push
Download latest version from GitHub: git pull
git status

repeat #1-8

title: Version control & Git
text:
Which files to track?
Depends on your aims. Usually:
Track:

source files (files that are created and edited by hand: scripts, raw data, metadata)
derived products with external value (e.g., figures, tables, reports)
configuration files (e.g., .Rproj, .gitignore)

Ignore:

intermediates (e.g. log files, temporary files generated from source files)

title: Version control & Git
text:
Prerequisites for happy ‘gitting’

have git installed
have your credentials configured on your local machine
have a GUI that you like and feel comfortable with

I like the built-in git GUI in Visual Studio Code but also use GitHub Desktop and the RStudio-panel

establish a routine (commit frequently, push often)
if you switch between different machines or collaborate with others always start with synchronizing the changes to your current machine pull or fetch

title: Version control & Git
section: Establish a routine when working solo
text:
Establish a routine when working solo

use projects (R projects, Python projects, Positron folders/projects, VSC workspaces), i.e., dedicate a specific folder to each project
initialize local folders as git repositories
initialize new folders for future projects directly as git repositories
stage changes that you want to keep
commit them to the repository and write a summary what was changed (annotation!!)
split commits thematically into smaller bits
big change: create a branch

if you are happy: merge the branch into your main branch
if you are not happy: delete, archive, or ignore and switch back to main

after a milestone is reached or at the end of the day: push
when working on different machines or editing files via the web browser: pull often to avoid critical errors
use issues on GitHub to track your own to-dos for your project

title: Good to know when working with Git
text:
Never link a cloud folder to git (e.g., Box, OneDrive, Dropbox, Google Drive) as it will mess up your cloud folder AND your git.
Never make commits of many files as once. It will be useless when you want to go back to a previous version. Only commit files together that are related to each other or depend on the same kind of change. If you are working on a project with multiple people, it is even more important to make small commits.
Never store very large data on GitHub. There are limits to the size of files. If you want some medium-sized files in Git, initalize the repository with Git Large File Storage (LFS). If you have very large files, consider using a cloud storage service (e.g., Box, OneDrive, Dropbox, Google Drive) and link to them in your repository.
Git is not a backup solution. It is a version control system. Make sure to have a backup of your data in case something goes wrong. Remember that only files that you commit to git will be “backed up”. Raw data is usually not committed to git - so your project becomes useless if you rely on git for backup. Removing files from git will remove them from your local folder as well. You can delete repositories on GitHub and they will be gone forever. Make sure to have a backup of your data in case something goes wrong.
Never commit any credentials/passwords to git. If you do, they will be public and anyone can access your accounts. Use environment variables or a separate configuration file that is not tracked by git to store sensitive information. If it happens - you have to delete the whole repository from GitHub and create a new one.
Never ignore your .gitignore! Do some research which files can be excluded from git depending on your project, coding language and workflow. You can find out which files to ignore by searing on gitignore.io





When creating a new project tick the “initalize as git repository” box
If you want to convert a local folder into a git repo use “New project” > “New project” > “version control”
You will get a new panel “Git” or “SVN” (By default: upper right panel - where your environment is)
You can see changes, stage, commit, push, pull from there





Source Control panel on the left
“Synchronize” is a function that first pulls and then pushes your changes. It’s useful to avoid running into conflicts





If you are a Windows user, make sure to set the line endings to LF in your git settings (when appropriate..) or convert a windows-made file to LF using: dos2unix [FILENAME]. (How do I do that? See here.)
Things are way easier for non-Windows users: Line endings (CRLF in windowns vs. LF in Unix-systems) can cause warnings and unnecessary complications when working with git. If you are a Windows user, make sure to set the line endings to LF in your git settings (when appropriate..) or convert a windows-made file to LF using: dos2unix [FILENAME]. (How do I do that? See here.)
Windows users: If you use WSL for some projects (e.g. bash coding) make sure to set up your project within WSL and initate it as git repository there. Avoid setting up the project folder in Windows and trying to use it in WSL. This will cause problems like slow performance, file permission issues, line-ending problems, issues with symbolic links, inconsistent behaviour of linux tools (especially when using R projects, python virtual environments, conda environments, nexflow pipelines, and bioinformatic workflows that creates thousands of files)
Set up your git on WSL is an extra step!





Branches are a great way to work on new features or changes without affecting the main codebase.
Always create a new branch for each new feature or change you are working on.
When your changes are ready, you can merge the branch back into the main branch (usually called main or master).
This helps keep the main branch stable and allows for easier collaboration with others.
To bring your changes back to the main branch, you need to make a pull request. The goal is to review the changes and make sure you are not accidentally overwriting or deleting files.
3 Types of pull requests: Source and more Details

Merge commit:


preserves branch commits and records the merge


Squash merge:


Adds one combined commit to the target branch


Rebase merge:


Adds the new branch at the end of the main branch (makes a linear history)






Perks of GitHub: The community!
Functionality
GitHub Copilot Student (Pro access via the university)
Markdown 🤝 GitHub
quick publish a website by creating an index.qmd, render it to .html and push to github. Will be [Your-User-Name].github.io/[repository name] (requirement: public repository)
Wikis! -> provide longer-term guidance across multiple topics
You can set up repositories as templates and then whenever you want to start a new project you can clone your template repo and don’t have to spend time on setting up the same folder structures over and over




Easy workflow to get a website for your repository in less than a minute and with less than 10 steps! Prerequisites: use Markdown or Quarto

create a new project (either chose ‘website’ if you want the whole repo to become a website OR create a normal R project)
create a new file, either: a) RMarkdown b) Quarto (works similar. Markdown is old, Quarto is new and has more functionalities and it has lots of shortcuts for formating and making things look pretty without knowledge of CSS)
save it as index.qmd (quarto) or index.rmd (RMarkdown) or index.md (markdown) to your root folder
knit (markdown) or render (quarto) your document (there is a button or use: quarto render index.qmd)
initalize the git repository: switch from R Console to Bash Terminal git add -A (-A adds/stages all files) and then git commit -am 'add webpage' and git push
Return to github, find your repository there; go to ‘Settings’ on your repository page
Find “Pages” on the left
we will “deploy from branch” and the branch is currently “main”. So we chose the main branch and use the /root folder.
Wait for the website to become live, there is a banner on top of the GitHub pages page that shows you the status and link of your website.
DONE!





You can totally exploit most functions in GitHub for your own work.
“Issues” on github are usually related to bugs in the code or questions from users if something does not work. This doesn’t have to be the case if you work alone (although it can be)
You can use Issues as a task tracker for your projects. Tasks should be actionable: 1) what job has to be done 2) are there dependecies to consider 3) Who will do it (if you are working alone - this does not matter too much) 4) How long will each task take? 5) What should be the result?
Issues has discussions attached so you can comment on them.
Once the task has been completed you can close the issue.
“Labels” show recurring tags such as Type, Status, Priority
